learnerMessages.intro-1: China, 1980. There is no phone in your pocket, no translator in your bag, and nobody on this street who speaks your language: whatever you have to say, you will say it in Chinese.
learnerMessages.intro-2: You have { $currency }{ $wallet }. There is a room for you down the street; the rent, { $currency }{ $rent }, falls due at the end of each week, and food costs money every day.
learnerMessages.intro-3: There is work in the noodle shop, at the warehouse, out on the road. It needs words, and words get you paid in full only when you get them right the first time.
learnerMessages.intro-4: On a bench by the road an old man is watching you with open curiosity. Maybe start there.
learnerMessages.setting-type-prompt: Type it in Chinese or pinyin:
learnerMessages.place-street-desc: Bikes, steam, and an old man on a bench.
learnerMessages.place-noodle_shop-desc: Steam everywhere, and the cook shouting orders at nobody.
learnerMessages.place-room-desc: A narrow bed, a window on the street, and a landlord who hears every step.
learnerMessages.place-market-desc: Stalls, scooters, and a warehouse with its doors open.
learnerMessages.place-station_road-desc: A wide road down to the station, a tea house steaming on the corner.
learnerMessages.place-school-desc: Children's voices through the open windows, and a teacher at the gate.
learnerMessages.place-hospital-desc: White walls, a long queue, and a doctor hurrying past.
learnerMessages.place-station-desc: Announcements you can't follow, people with too much luggage, and a taxi driver shouting for fares.
learnerMessages.place-shop-desc: Shelves to the ceiling, a crate of apples by the door, and a shopkeeper who misses nothing.
learnerMessages.place-warehouse-desc: Stacks of tables and chairs, and a big man with a clipboard.
learnerMessages.npc-wang-desc: Sits on a bench on Main Street all day, and talks to anyone who stops, whether they understand him or not.
learnerMessages.npc-cook-desc: Runs the noodle shop, shouts orders at nobody, and pays in cash when the last bowl goes out.
learnerMessages.npc-landlord-desc: Thin, in slippers, and hears every step on the stairs. Rent is on his mind.
learnerMessages.npc-foreman-desc: A big man with a clipboard at the warehouse, who hires anyone who can count.
learnerMessages.npc-dispatcher-desc: Runs a stall of parcels on Market Street and always needs someone to carry one.
learnerMessages.npc-doctor-desc: Always on the way to somewhere else, until you're the one in the chair.
learnerMessages.npc-teacher-desc: Teaches Chinese to grown-ups at the school, and writes every name on the class list.
learnerMessages.npc-traveller-desc: Waiting at the station with one eye on the Beijing train.
learnerMessages.npc-shopkeeper-desc: Keeps the corner shop and its abacus, and misses nothing.
learnerMessages.scene-street-hello-start: The old man pats the bench beside him. Stuck? Press [w] to look a word up.
learnerMessages.scene-street-hello-end: Old Wang looks delighted, and repeats your name, getting it wrong each time.
learnerMessages.scene-street-hungry-start: Your stomach growls, and Old Wang raises an eyebrow.
learnerMessages.scene-street-hungry-end: Old Wang points down the street at a noodle shop: his friend Xiao Zhang cooks there.
learnerMessages.scene-street-practice-start: Old Wang waves you back over: greet him, mind your manners, then say goodbye properly.
learnerMessages.scene-street-practice-end: Old Wang beams, satisfied you've finally got your manners right.
learnerMessages.scene-street-numbers-start: Old Wang holds up his fingers: time to learn to count.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-bowl-start: Steam rolls out of the door. The cook glances up from her pot and waves you to a stool.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-bowl-end: She waves your money away: Old Wang's friends eat free, once. Then she's back at the pot, shouting orders she has nobody to count out.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-intro-start: Xiao Zhang looks you up and down, wiping her hands: a customer, or a pair of hands?
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-intro-end: She throws you an apron: you have a job.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-shift-start: Xiao Zhang shoves you toward the counter and starts shouting orders: fetch drinks, serve customers.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-shift-end: The last order goes out. Xiao Zhang wipes her hands and pays you.
learnerMessages.scene-room-hello-start: A thin man in slippers opens the door before you knock.
learnerMessages.scene-room-hello-end: Mr Li hands you a key on a red string: the room is yours.
learnerMessages.scene-room-rent-start: Mr Li waits at the top of the stairs, rubbing his fingers together.
learnerMessages.scene-room-rent-end: Mr Li nods and writes fifty on his hand. It's due every week.
learnerMessages.scene-warehouse-intro-start: The big man with the clipboard raises an eyebrow: can you count?
learnerMessages.scene-warehouse-intro-end: Big Liu writes something on his clipboard, possibly your name.
learnerMessages.scene-warehouse-shift-start: Big Liu points at the furniture and calls out what to carry. Do what he says.
learnerMessages.scene-warehouse-shift-end: Shift over. Big Liu counts the pieces and pays you.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-intro-start: A young woman at a stall piled with parcels waves you over.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-intro-end: Miss Gao writes your name on a parcel label, then holds the parcel out to you.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-pickup-start: Miss Gao slaps a parcel down: say where it's going, then get moving before she changes her mind.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-hospital-start: The doctor at the desk looks up: say who you're delivering for, then hand the parcel over.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-hospital-end: The doctor signs your slip. Delivery done.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-school-start: The teacher waiting by the gate holds out a hand: say who sent you, then the books.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-school-end: The teacher takes the books and signs your slip. Delivery done.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-station-start: The traveller checks his watch: say who you're looking for, and when the Beijing train leaves.
learnerMessages.scene-delivery-station-end: He thanks you and hurries off. Delivery done.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-kitchen-start: Xiao Zhang waves you to the sink: wash cups, grab a bite, then get back out front.
learnerMessages.scene-noodle-kitchen-end: You dry your hands and head out to buy more cups.
learnerMessages.scene-shop-intro-start: The shopkeeper looks up from her abacus as you come in.
learnerMessages.scene-shop-intro-end: You leave with one apple, and the feeling you paid too much anyway.
learnerMessages.scene-shop-buy-start: The shopkeeper eyes the shelves: name what you want, and the price, before she'll sell it.
learnerMessages.scene-shop-buy-end: You count coins into her hand and step back out onto the street.

learnerMessages.note-hao-ma: 好 (hǎo) means "good", and on its own it's how you agree: "OK". Put 吗 (ma) at the end of a sentence and it becomes a yes-or-no question: 你好吗？ is "How are you?", literally "You good?" The usual answer is 很好 (hěn hǎo), "very good"; the 很 is there mostly for rhythm.
learnerMessages.note-lao-xiao: Friends and neighbours your own age are often called by surname with 老 (lǎo, "old") or 小 (xiǎo, "little") in front: 老王 for someone a bit older, 小张 for someone younger. From a young stranger to an old man it would be too familiar; you'd say 王大爷, "Grandpa Wang". Old Wang told you to call him 老王, which is his way of saying you're friends now.
learnerMessages.note-le: 了 (le) after a word often marks a change: 我饿了 is "I've got hungry", "I'm hungry now". You'll also hear it in 太好了！, "great!", literally "too good!"
learnerMessages.note-bukeqi: 谢谢 (xièxie) is "thank you". The usual answer is 不客气 (bùkèqi), "you're welcome"; it literally means "don't be polite": no need to stand on ceremony. Between close friends, people often skip 谢谢 altogether; thanking a friend too much can sound distant.
learnerMessages.note-bei: Chinese doesn't say "three teas". A measure word goes between a number and a thing: 三杯茶 is "three cups of tea". 杯 (bēi) is the one for cups and glasses. There are many measure words; 个 (gè) is the everyday all-purpose one.
learnerMessages.note-ge: 个 (gè) is the measure word you can use for almost anything: 八个椅子, "eight chairs". For two of something, say 两 (liǎng), not 二: 两个桌子. 二 is for counting and for numbers like 十二. Strictly, chairs take 把 (bǎ) and tables take 张 (zhāng), but 个 is always understood.
learnerMessages.note-kuai: Prices on a sign say 元 (yuán), but people say 块 (kuài): 五十块 is fifty yuan. 多少钱？ is "how much?", literally "how much money?"
learnerMessages.note-nali-title: 哪里, 那里, 这里
learnerMessages.note-nali: 哪里 (nǎli) is "where", 那里 (nàli) "there" and 这里 (zhèli) "here": 学校在哪里？ is "where is the school?". In the north people say 哪儿, 那儿 and 这儿 (nǎr, nàr, zhèr). They mean the same.
learnerMessages.note-de: 的 (de) joins an owner to a thing: 高小姐的朋友 is "Miss Gao's friend", and 医院的东西 is "the hospital's things".
learnerMessages.note-dian: 点 (diǎn) after a number gives the hour: 三点 is three o'clock, and 现在几点？ asks "what time is it?". The 了 in 三点了 means "it's three already".
learnerMessages.note-mei: 没有 (méiyǒu) is "don't have" or "there isn't": 杯子没有了 is "we're out of cups". Most verbs take 不 for "not", but 有 always takes 没: 没有, never 不有.
learnerMessages.note-tai: 太 (tài) … 了 means "too …": 太多了 is "that's too much". The 了 at the end is part of the pattern. For prices people usually say 太贵了 (tài guì le), "too expensive".
learnerMessages.note-hui-neng: 会 (huì) is "can" for a skill you learned: 我会写字, "I can write characters". 能 (néng) is "can" because nothing stops you: 你能来吗？, "can you come?". So 不会 means you never learned it, and 不能 means you can't right now.
learnerMessages.note-zai: Before a place, 在 (zài) means "at": 我在学校. Before an action it means "in the middle of doing it": 猫在睡觉 is "the cat is sleeping", and 谁在说话？ is "who's talking?".

learnerMessages.intro-1: Tokyo, 1995. Your bag was stolen on the first night, with your passport in it, and the embassy says a new one takes weeks. There is no phone in your pocket and nobody on this street speaks your language: whatever you have to say, you will say it in Japanese.
learnerMessages.intro-2: You have { $currency }{ $wallet }. A landlady down the street has a room; the rent, { $currency }{ $rent }, falls due at the end of each week, and food costs money every day.
learnerMessages.intro-3: The ramen shop is short of hands. It needs words, and words get you paid in full only when you get them right the first time.
learnerMessages.intro-4: On a bench under the arcade roof an old man is feeding pigeons and watching you. Maybe start there.
learnerMessages.setting-type-prompt: Type it in Japanese or rōmaji:
learnerMessages.place-shotengai-desc: A covered arcade of small shops, bicycles, and an old man on a bench.
learnerMessages.place-apartment-desc: Six tatami mats, a futon, and a landlady who hears every step.
learnerMessages.place-ramen-desc: Eight stools at a counter, steam, and an owner who talks while he cooks.
learnerMessages.place-konbini-desc: Bright light, a chime at the door, and rice balls in neat rows.
learnerMessages.scene-tanaka-hello: Say hello to the old man
learnerMessages.scene-tanaka-hello-start: The old man pats the bench beside him. Stuck? Press [w] to look a word up.
learnerMessages.scene-tanaka-hello-end: Mr Tanaka nods, satisfied, and goes back to his pigeons.
learnerMessages.scene-tanaka-name-start: Mr Tanaka taps his chest, then points at you.
learnerMessages.scene-tanaka-name-end: Mr Tanaka says your name over to himself, twice, as if filing it away.
learnerMessages.scene-tanaka-numbers-start: Mr Tanaka holds up his fingers: time to learn to count.
learnerMessages.scene-apartment-hello-start: A small woman in an apron opens the door before you knock.
learnerMessages.scene-apartment-hello-end: The landlady hands you a key on a wooden tag: the room is yours.
learnerMessages.scene-apartment-rent-start: The landlady waits in the doorway with a notebook.
learnerMessages.scene-apartment-rent-end: The landlady writes 5,000 on a slip of paper and tapes it to your door. It's due every week.
learnerMessages.scene-ramen-intro-start: A man in a white headband waves you in from behind the counter.
learnerMessages.scene-ramen-intro-end: The owner ties a towel round your head: you have a job.
learnerMessages.scene-ramen-shift-start: The owner shouts over the noise: fetch drinks, then serve them as the orders come in.
learnerMessages.scene-ramen-shift-end: The last bowl goes out. The owner wipes down the counter and pays you.
learnerMessages.scene-konbini-prices-start: The door chimes. A young clerk in a striped uniform bows.
learnerMessages.scene-konbini-prices-end: The clerk bows again as you leave. The rice balls are 150 yen.
learnerMessages.scene-konbini-buy-start: The clerk waits behind the counter: say what you want, then thank her when she rings it up.
learnerMessages.scene-konbini-buy-end: She bags your item and bows. Another sale done.

learnerMessages.note-desu-masu: Polite sentences end in です (desu, "is") or a verb in its ます (masu) form: わかります, "I understand". Change ます to ません for "not": わかりません. To strangers, shopkeepers and your landlady, stay polite; the plain forms are for friends.
learnerMessages.note-tsu: For counting things, one to nine, Japanese has its own numbers ending in つ (tsu): 一つ hitotsu, 二つ futatsu, 三つ mittsu, 四つ yottsu, 五つ itsutsu. They work for almost anything: お茶を二つ, "two teas". Prices and money use the other numbers: 五百円, gohyaku en.
learnerMessages.note-wa-ga: は (written "ha", said wa) marks what you're talking about: わたしは…です, "as for me, I'm …". が (ga) marks the thing itself, often something new or asked about: お金がありません, "there's no money". When in doubt, は for "as for", が before あります.
learnerMessages.note-o: を (written "wo", said o) marks the thing an action is done to: お茶をください, "tea, please" (literally "please give tea"); ラーメンを食べます, "I eat ramen". It comes straight after the thing.
